medical_disclaimer: These movement prompts are general information for adults who can exercise safely. They do not diagnose, treat, prevent, or rehabilitate any condition. If you have an injury, recent surgery, osteoporosis, significant balance impairment, or another condition affecting exercise, ask a qualified clinician which movements are suitable.
global_safety: Use a stable, non-wheeled chair and a clear floor area. Move slowly, breathe normally, and stay within a comfortable range. Do not bounce, force a joint, or continue through pain. Stop for pain, severe discomfort, dizziness, chest discomfort, unusual breathlessness, numbness, or loss of balance.
media_provenance: The bundled videos are language-neutral generated demonstrations created for Vulture. They contain no narration, text, logos, or footage of a real person. Most use the shared mannequin style; a minimal geometric fallback remains where a reviewed mannequin replacement is not yet available. The generation prompts and review requirements are included in video-prompts.json; the movement guidance and doses are tied to the cited evidence sources.

sources.title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour
sources.supports: Limit sedentary time and replace it with physical activity of any intensity; it does not define a precise break interval.

sources.organization: US Occupational Safety and Health Administration
sources.title: Computer Workstations: Work Process and Recognition
sources.supports: A five-minute break from computer tasks every hour may include looking away, stretching, standing, or walking.

sources.organization: Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety
sources.title: Office Ergonomics: Stretching at the Workstation
sources.supports: Workstation-break guidance, shoulder shrug and wrist movement doses, and general stretching precautions.

sources.title: Sitting exercises
sources.supports: Stable-chair precautions and the specified chest stretch, hip marching, and ankle point-and-flex instructions and doses.

sources.title: Strength exercises
sources.supports: The specified sit-to-stand and supported calf-raise instructions and doses.

sources.title: Effects of Interrupting Prolonged Sitting with Physical Activity Breaks: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
sources.supports: Activity breaks improve acute glucose and insulin outcomes compared with uninterrupted sitting; optimal timing and long-term implications remain uncertain.

sources.title: Effects of prolonged sitting, prolonged standing, and activity breaks: a randomised crossover trial
sources.supports: In a small acute trial, two-minute walking breaks every 30 minutes outperformed uninterrupted sitting or prolonged standing for selected insulin and blood-flow outcomes.

sources.title: The Acute Effects of Interrupting Prolonged Sitting Time in Adults with Standing and Light-Intensity Walking on Biomarkers of Cardiometabolic Health in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
sources.supports: Acute randomized crossover evidence suggests that light walking produces larger post-meal glucose and insulin effects than standing alone; long-term clinical outcomes were not established.

sources.title: Give me a break! A systematic review and meta-analysis on the efficacy of micro-breaks for increasing well-being and performance
sources.supports: Micro-breaks under ten minutes improved vigor and fatigue on average; performance findings depended on task and break length.

sources.title: Working safely with display screen equipment: Work routine and breaks
sources.supports: Short, frequent breaks or changes of activity are preferred; users should move around, stretch, or change posture, and exact timing depends on the work.

sources.title: Computer vision syndrome
sources.supports: Recommends the 20-20-20 distance-view guideline, frequent blinking, regular rest breaks, and screen-position adjustments for digital eye strain.

sources.title: 20-20-20 Rule: Are These Numbers Justified?
sources.supports: A small controlled study found no significant symptom or task-performance benefit from scheduled 20-second breaks, so the exact 20-20-20 timing should not be presented as proven treatment.

sources.title: Effectiveness of workplace exercise interventions for musculoskeletal disorders in office workers: systematic review
sources.supports: Workplace exercise may reduce pain, but heterogeneous studies and high risk of bias prevent firm treatment or prevention claims.

sources.title: Frequency of Interruptions to Sitting Time: Benefits for Postprandial Metabolism in Type 2 Diabetes
sources.supports: In 23 adults with medication-controlled type 2 diabetes, six minutes of simple resistance activities each hour reduced acute post-meal glucose and insulin compared with uninterrupted sitting; the study does not validate shorter isolated prompts or long-term outcomes.

sources.organization: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
sources.title: Optimal Frequency of Interrupting Prolonged Sitting for Cardiometabolic Health: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Crossover Trials
sources.supports: Higher-frequency interruptions, at least every 30 minutes, showed a modest glucose advantage over less frequent interruptions, but the certainty of evidence was low and other outcomes did not differ significantly.

sources.title: Effectiveness of micro-exercises for managing neck/shoulder pain in sedentary workers: a systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.supports: Repeated workplace micro-exercise programs may improve neck and shoulder pain and disability, but certainty ranged from moderate to very low, heterogeneity was high, and isolated reminder doses were not tested.

sources.title: Brief structured respiration practices enhance mood and reduce physiological arousal
sources.supports: A remote randomized trial found that daily five-minute breathwork, especially exhale-focused cyclic sighing, improved mood and reduced respiratory rate; one optional reminder is not a treatment protocol.

sources.title: 40-second green roof views sustain attention: The role of micro-breaks in attention restoration
sources.supports: A laboratory study of 150 students found fewer sustained-attention lapses after a 40-second green-roof view than after a concrete-roof view; this is a promising single study rather than a universal prescription.

exercises.title: Easy desk-side walk
exercises.short_prompt: Walk at a comfortable pace for five minutes.
steps: Stand only if it is safe for you to do so.
Walk at a comfortable pace around the room or corridor.
Keep the route clear, use your usual walking aid, and breathe normally.
exercises.safety: Skip this movement if you feel unsteady. Stop for pain, dizziness, chest discomfort, or unusual breathlessness.
exercises.evidence_note: The five-minute dose follows OSHA's hourly computer-task break guidance. WHO and the systematic review support replacing sedentary time with movement, but do not establish this exact interval as a medical prescription.

exercises.title: Seated chest stretch
exercises.short_prompt: Open the chest gently while seated.
steps: Sit upright and away from the chair back.
Draw your shoulders back and down, then extend your arms to the sides.
Gently move your chest forward and up, hold, and release.
exercises.safety: Move only to gentle tension. Do not force the shoulders. Stop if the movement causes pain.
exercises.evidence_note: Instructions and dose follow the NHS sitting-exercises guidance.

exercises.title: Shoulder shrug and release
exercises.short_prompt: Raise your shoulders gently, then let them relax.
steps: Keep your head facing forward and breathe normally.
Raise both shoulders toward your ears until you feel slight tension.
Hold briefly, then let the shoulders relax fully downward.
exercises.safety: Keep the movement slow. Do not force it or hold your breath. Stop for pain or severe discomfort.
exercises.evidence_note: Instructions and dose follow CCOHS workstation-stretching guidance.

exercises.title: Gentle wrist side-bend
exercises.short_prompt: Move each wrist gently from side to side.
exercises.dose: Hold each side 3-5 seconds; 3 cycles per wrist
steps: Open one hand with the palm facing down.
Move the wrist gently from side to side within a comfortable range.
Pause at each end, then repeat with the other wrist.
exercises.safety: Do not push the hand with your other hand. Stop if pain, tingling, or numbness appears.
exercises.evidence_note: Instructions and dose follow CCOHS workstation-stretching guidance.

exercises.title: Seated hip marching
exercises.short_prompt: Lift one bent knee at a time while seated.
steps: Sit upright on a stable, non-wheeled chair without leaning back.
Hold the sides of the chair.
Lift one bent knee as far as comfortable, lower it with control, and alternate.
exercises.safety: Keep the movement comfortable and do not force the hip. Stop if it causes pain.
contraindication_flags: recent hip surgery without clinical clearance
exercises.evidence_note: Instructions and dose follow the NHS sitting-exercises guidance.

exercises.title: Seated ankle point and flex
exercises.short_prompt: Point and flex one foot at a time.
steps: Sit upright and hold the sides of a stable chair.
Straighten one leg so the foot is off the floor.
Point the toes away, then draw them back toward you; repeat on the other side.
exercises.safety: Move slowly without forcing the ankle. One-sided calf pain or swelling may need urgent medical assessment rather than exercise.
contraindication_flags: unexplained one-sided calf pain or swelling
exercises.evidence_note: Instructions and dose follow the NHS sitting-exercises guidance.

exercises.title: Sit-to-stand
exercises.short_prompt: Stand up and sit down slowly five times.
steps: Use a stable chair that cannot roll or slip and sit near its front edge.
Place your feet hip-width apart, lean slightly forward, and stand slowly using your legs.
Stand upright, then sit down slowly; use your hands only as much as needed.
exercises.safety: Choose a seated movement instead if standing is unsafe or you have significant balance problems.
exercises.evidence_note: Instructions and dose follow the NHS strength-exercises guidance.

exercises.title: Supported calf raise
exercises.short_prompt: Rise onto your toes while holding a stable chair.
steps: Stand behind a stable chair and hold its back with both hands.
Slowly lift both heels as far as comfortable.
Lower both heels with control and repeat.
exercises.safety: Keep holding the chair. Stop if you become unsteady or develop pain.
exercises.evidence_note: Instructions and dose follow the supported version in NHS strength-exercises guidance; the app does not show the unsupported progression.

exercises.title: Head glide
exercises.short_prompt: Draw your head gently back without lifting the chin.
exercises.dose: Hold briefly; repeat up to 5 times
steps: Sit or stand upright with your gaze level.
Keep the chin level and glide the head straight back, as if making a small double chin.
Pause without forcing the range, then release fully.
exercises.safety: Keep the movement small and slow. Stop for pain, dizziness, tingling, numbness, or other unusual symptoms.
exercises.evidence_note: The technique follows CCOHS workstation guidance. The review supports repeated workplace micro-exercise programs broadly, not this isolated movement as treatment.

exercises.title: Shoulder-blade squeeze
exercises.short_prompt: Bring the shoulder blades gently toward one another.
exercises.dose: Hold up to 5 seconds; repeat up to 5 times
steps: Sit or stand tall with your arms relaxed.
Let the shoulders stay low as you draw the shoulder blades gently together.
Hold briefly, breathe normally, and release.
exercises.safety: Use only a comfortable range. Stop if the neck or shoulders become painful.
exercises.evidence_note: The technique and conservative dose follow CCOHS workstation guidance. The review does not validate one isolated reminder dose.

exercises.title: Slow shoulder rolls
exercises.short_prompt: Circle the shoulders slowly in both directions.
steps: Let your arms hang easily and keep your head facing forward.
Roll both shoulders slowly backward five times.
Pause, then roll them slowly forward five times.
exercises.safety: Keep the circles comfortable and unforced. Stop if the movement causes pain.
exercises.evidence_note: The technique follows CCOHS workstation guidance. Evidence for repeated workplace programs should not be read as proof that one shoulder-roll prompt treats pain.

exercises.title: Finger opening sequence
exercises.short_prompt: Move slowly from an open hand into a gentle fist and back.
steps: Open one hand and spread the fingers without straining.
Make a gentle fist with the thumb resting outside the fingers.
Slide the fingertips toward the base of the fingers, then open the hand again.
Repeat with the other hand.
exercises.safety: Do not force the fingers with the other hand. Stop for pain, tingling, or numbness.
exercises.evidence_note: The sequence and conservative dose follow CCOHS workstation guidance.

exercises.title: Simple resistance circuit
exercises.short_prompt: Combine a few supported lower-body movements in one calm round.
steps: Stand behind a stable chair with a clear floor around you.
Complete up to 5 shallow supported mini-squats.
Complete up to 5 supported calf raises.
Lift one knee at a time for up to 5 lifts per side.
Finish with 5 gentle tighten-and-release contractions around the hips and buttocks.
exercises.safety: Use stable support and a comfortable range. Choose a seated movement if standing is unsafe or unsteady.
exercises.evidence_note: The trial used longer six-minute hourly circuits in adults with medication-controlled type 2 diabetes. Vulture offers a shorter sampler for activity variation and does not claim the trial's metabolic effect.
